title: Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti
text:
This profile draws on publicly available professional sources (see references below) rather than an internal staff submission. If you are Prof. Datti or write on his behalf and would like to correct or expand this page, please contact the department.
Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti (also published as Alhassan Datti Mohammed and Alhassan Mohammed Datti) is the most senior consultant in the Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care at Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital, and one of the pioneering anaesthetists of Kano and Jigawa States.

title: Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti
text:
Training
Prof. Datti trained in anaesthesia from 1997 to 2003 at the University of Ibadan and University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan — Nigeria’s oldest teaching hospital — where he obtained the Postgraduate Diploma in Anaesthesia. He went on to become a Fellow of the West African College of Surgeons (WACS) in Anaesthesia in 2007, the first Fellow of the College from either Kano or Jigawa State in Northwest Nigeria.

title: Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti
text:
Work and interests
Prof. Datti’s career has combined clinical anaesthesia with public-health research and regional capacity-building:

He served as principal investigator on a study, conducted with PRRINN‑MNCH (Partnership for Reviving Routine Immunisation in Northern Nigeria — Maternal, Newborn and Child Health), examining the impact of access to safe, reliable general anaesthesia on emergency obstetric care and neonatal outcomes.
He documented AKTH’s transition from ketamine-only to inhalational general anaesthesia, and has spoken on this experience at international meetings, including the All‑Africa Anaesthesia Congress.
He coordinated a partnership between the Liberian Dental Association, the Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists, and AKTH to train Liberian physicians toward the WACS Diploma in Anaesthesia (DA), addressing a critical shortage of physician anaesthesia providers in Liberia.
He has co-authored multiple peer-reviewed studies from the department, spanning obstetric anaesthesia, patient knowledge and perception of anaesthesia, and drug-dosing research relevant to routine practice in a resource-constrained setting.

title: Prof. Alhassan Muhammad Datti
text:
Leadership beyond the department
Prof. Datti also served as President-Elect of the Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists (2022–2024 Executive Committee).

title: Acute Post-Operative Pain Management: A Departmental Seminar
text:
Overview
This seminar covered the principles of multimodal analgesia for post-operative pain, the department’s acute pain service workflow, and common pitfalls in prescribing opioid and non-opioid analgesia on surgical wards.
Topics included:

The WHO analgesic ladder, adapted for acute post-operative pain
Multimodal analgesia — combining paracetamol, NSAIDs (where not contraindicated), and regional techniques to reduce opioid requirement
Recognising and managing opioid-related side effects on the ward
When to escalate to the acute pain service

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
text:
Departmental guide
Prepared by the Residents’ Academic Committee
Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital
KEYWORDS · REGIONAL ANAESTHESIA · ULTRASOUND · NERVE BLOCKS · TRAINING

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
text:
1 Probe selection

Linear (high-frequency) probes — best for superficial structures (nerves within ~4 cm), such as interscalene, supraclavicular, and forearm blocks. Better resolution, less penetration.
Curvilinear (low-frequency) probes — needed for deeper structures, such as the sciatic nerve at the gluteal level or in larger patients.

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
text:
2 Needle visualisation

In-plane technique keeps the entire needle shaft visible along the probe’s long axis — generally the easier technique to learn first, as the needle tip position is continuously seen.
Out-of-plane technique shows the needle only as a bright dot crossing the beam — faster for some experienced operators, but easier to lose track of the tip as a beginner.
Small, deliberate needle movements — rather than large sweeps — make it far easier to keep the tip in view.

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
text:
3 Common early pitfalls

Chasing the needle with the probe instead of keeping the probe still and adjusting the needle trajectory — this usually makes tip tracking worse, not better.
Mistaking the needle shadow for the tip — the brightest point on screen is not always the true tip; small in-and-out jiggles or a burst of local anaesthetic (hydrolocation) can help confirm true tip position.
Poor gel contact at the probe edges, distorting the image exactly where the needle is entering.

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
section: 4 Grounding this in the wider training literature
text:
4 Grounding this in the wider training literature
This orientation guide is meant as a first-days primer, not a substitute for a structured training pathway. The joint ASRA/ESRA committee recommendations describe a full residency- and fellowship-based training pathway for ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia, including the core technical competencies and the didactic and experiential components expected before independent practice (Sites et al. 2009) — residents progressing beyond this primer should be familiar with that pathway.

title: Getting Started with Point-of-Care Ultrasound for Regional Anaesthesia
text:
5 Using this guide
This is an orientation aid, not a replacement for supervised practice. Residents should complete ultrasound-guided blocks under direct consultant supervision until independently competent, per departmental training requirements.

title: Welcome to the Department Blog
text:
Why this site exists
Anaesthesia and intensive care are, by nature, quiet specialties — much of our best work happens behind the drapes or at the bedside, rarely seen by the wider hospital community. This site is a small window into that work: who we are, what we do, and how we continue to learn. In many ways, anaesthesiologists are the unsung heroes of the medical profession.
We look forward to sharing more soon.

title: About the Department
text:
Our mission

To deliver safe, compassionate and evidence-based anaesthesia and critical care, while training clinicians who will extend that same standard of care across Nigeria.

title: About the Department
text:
What we do

Clinical anaesthesia — general, regional, obstetric and paediatric anaesthesia for elective and emergency surgery.
Intensive care — multidisciplinary critical care for medical, surgical and obstetric patients requiring organ support.
Pain management — acute post-operative pain services and chronic pain referral clinics.
Resuscitation & emergency response — peri-arrest and trauma resuscitation support hospital-wide.
Postgraduate training — a structured residency programme leading to Fellowship of the West African College of Surgeons (WACS) and the National Postgraduate Medical College of Nigeria (NPMCN).
Research & continuing education — audits, quality-improvement projects and regular departmental CPD, in step with NSA and WFSA guidance.

title: A Simple ICU Ward Round Checklist Worth Repeating
text: Structured checklists reduce missed items on busy multidisciplinary ward rounds. Many departments use a version of the FAST HUG mnemonic, and it remains a useful teaching anchor for residents new to the intensive care unit:

title: A Simple ICU Ward Round Checklist Worth Repeating
text:
Using it well
A checklist is only useful if it prompts a genuine review rather than a box-ticking exercise. On our unit, the checklist is read aloud during the consultant-led round, with the bedside nurse and resident confirming each item against the patient in front of them — not from memory.
We will keep sharing short teaching notes like this one. If you have a topic you’d like covered, reach out to the department.

title: Marking World Anaesthesia Day at AKTH
text:
Every year on 16 October, the anaesthesia community marks World Anaesthesia Day, commemorating the first successful public demonstration of ether anaesthesia in 1846.
At AKTH, the department used the day to run a short in-house symposium for residents, nurse anaesthetists and theatre staff, focused on:

title: Marking World Anaesthesia Day at AKTH
text:
A shared global effort
Observances like this connect our department to the wider work of the Nigerian Society of Anaesthetists and the World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists, both of which promote safe anaesthesia access worldwide — a reminder that safe surgery and anaesthesia remain out of reach for many patients globally, and that local diligence contributes to a much larger effort.
Thank you to every member of the peri-operative team who took part.

title: A Practical Guide to Theatre-to-ICU Obstetric Handover
text:
Departmental guide
Prepared by the Residents’ Academic Committee
Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital
KEYWORDS · HANDOVER · OBSTETRIC ANAESTHESIA · PATIENT SAFETY · ICU ADMISSION

title: A Practical Guide to Theatre-to-ICU Obstetric Handover
text:
1 Why a structured handover matters
Verbal handovers that aren’t structured tend to omit items unpredictably — often exactly the detail that matters for the next few hours of care. A short, consistent structure reduces that risk without adding much time to a busy transfer. This mirrors the logic behind the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, which was shown to reduce post-operative morbidity and mortality across a range of hospital settings when used consistently (Haynes et al. 2009; Safe Surgery Saves Lives Study Group 2009).

title: A Practical Guide to Theatre-to-ICU Obstetric Handover
text:
2 Suggested handover structure

Patient identification & background — name, age, parity, key obstetric history, indication for surgery.
Procedure performed — type of anaesthesia, surgical procedure, any intra-operative complications.
Haemodynamic course — blood loss, fluids and blood products given, vasopressor use, any instability and how it was managed.
Airway and respiratory status — extubation status, oxygen requirement, any airway concerns for the ICU team to be aware of.
Analgesia plan — what has been given, what is prescribed next, and any regional technique in place (e.g. spinal opioid, wound catheter).
Outstanding concerns and thresholds for escalation — specifically what should prompt the ICU team to call anaesthesia back.

title: A Practical Guide to Theatre-to-ICU Obstetric Handover
text:
3 Using this guide
This is a teaching resource for residents, not a substitute for local protocol. Departments should adapt the sequence to match their own documentation and handover tools, and residents should confirm current local practice with their supervising consultant.
Have a guide, protocol summary, or teaching resource to contribute? Email the department to have it added here.

Topics included:

Pre-operative difficult airway prediction (Mallampati, thyromental distance, and their limitations)
The unanticipated difficult airway algorithm — plan A through D

Human factors in a crisis: communication and role allocation

title: Prof. Salahu Dalhat
text:
Research
Dr. Salahu is lead author, with departmental colleagues, of a 2021 study published in the Nigerian Journal of Medicine, and a co-author on two 2025 studies in the Nigerian Journal of Anaesthesia:

Salahu D, Adesope S, Datti AM, Miko Abdullahi M, Mamuda A, Mohammed AM. Efficacy of low-dose suxamethonium in reducing induction dose of propofol for laryngeal mask airway insertion in Nigerian adults. Nigerian Journal of Medicine, 2021;30:413–8.


Alhassan Z, Atiku M, Salahu D, Miko Abdullahi M, Datti Mohammad A. Burnout among Anaesthesia Providers in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Scoping Review. Nigerian Journal of Anaesthesia, 2025;2(2):77–86.

Full biography, qualifications, and areas of clinical interest to be added by the department.

text:

Dr. Zinnat Alhassan (published as Zynat Alhassan) is a member of the Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care at Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital.

title: Dr. Zinnat Alhassan
text:
Research
Dr. Alhassan is a co-author, alongside departmental colleagues, of two 2025 publications in the Nigerian Journal of Anaesthesia:

Alhassan Z, Atiku M, Salahu D, Miko Abdullahi M, Datti Mohammad A. Burnout among Anaesthesia Providers in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Scoping Review. Nigerian Journal of Anaesthesia, 2025;2(2):77–86. DOI: 10.82223/nja.vol2no2.50


Atiku M, Salahu D, Miko M. Abdullahi, Datti Mohammed A, Alhassan Z, Aminu AB. Graded Epidural Anaesthesia for Abdominal Hysterectomy in an Adult with Congenital Heart Disease: A Case Report. Nigerian Journal of Anaesthesia, 2025;2(2):114–116. DOI: 10.82223/nja.vol2no2.49
